checks: The radial Jacobian is H_X(1−r)^{d−1}, using d−1 tangent factors and the normal component of the radial derivative. Negative s_t supplies the outward shell with the required sign. For d=1 it is the signed interval length at each endpoint. The uniform radial bound and bounded equi-Lipschitz integrands give O(t²) replacement error, and H_X s_t/t→v in L¹ gives a uniform little-o remainder.

On each compact own-interior neighborhood an inball about every mark bounds the old and new projective parameters. The accepted denominator floor and O(t) Hausdorff distance make both sets of optimizers admissible for both bodies with a common floor on a fixed neighborhood. The objective convergence plus uniqueness proves uniform optimizer convergence by subsequences with converging marks. Evaluating the two objectives at old and new optimizers sandwiches the optimal values and yields the uniform coefficient −C_Y without differentiating the optimal parameter.

Independently differentiated log f=(log E+(log V_p)/d)/N−(log M)/d. The three terms give −C_Y/(NE_Y)−D_p/(dNV_p)+D/(dM). At fixed Γ-unit u, the centered second-moment derivative is −J(u), because the old within-fiber centered first moments vanish. After division by M and taking the square root this gives (D−J(u))/(2M). The log-scale contribution is s. Subtracting the full buffer gives the stated contact coefficient with +(J_i^{cov})/(2M) and −(d+2)D/(2dM).

An old interior contact remains feasible and gives an O(t) upper test value for the minimum. Compactness and profile continuity up to sampled boundaries put every limiting minimizer in the old finite zero set. On compact neighborhoods of these zeros the expansion is uniform and its coefficient is continuous; old nonnegativity gives the lower bound and testing all contacts gives the upper bound. The right derivative is the minimum of the contact coefficients.

Each selected cap crosses the interior of any assigned contact fiber at its old threshold. An old ball around a point of that plane leaves a smaller common ball after perturbation and provides a positive coarea floor throughout a fixed threshold interval. Other fibers contribute nonincreasing continuous tails even at support incidences. For each cap the two sides of the old threshold have masses bracketing Q, and retain the bracket for small t. On the common mass interval each local inverse is continuous and strictly decreasing. For two sufficiently near fixed masses on either side of Q the weighted inverse sum brackets h_i at t=0 and brackets h_i+α_i(t) for small t. This gives a unique q_i(t)→Q. Its defining equality forces at least one of the actual buffered thresholds at every assigned point to reach the corresponding inverse.

For off-I stability compare the old and moving cap masses using identical normals with Euclidean-unit continuous component. At aligned marks the threshold change is the own displacement plus the change in the ε f Γ term, with no dependence on base tilt. The common containing ball bounds the slab volume and the fiber symmetric differences bound the domain error. Pure-base cuts involve fixed base subsets. Taking infima yields convergence along all sequences of aligned marks, including boundary limits. Finite-base compactness then preserves the strict gap on the off-I bases while the continued masses tend to Q.

Exact interval calibration with d=1, one base and K=[−1,1]: let K(t)=[−R_t,R_t] with R_t=1−h t and either sign of h. At zero f_t(0)=1, the old Γ-unit normals are ±√3, thresholds are −ε, and weights are 1/2. The contact budget is exactly ε h t and q(t)=R_t(1+ε/√3) for ε<√3. Substitution of D=C=2h, J=6h, E=V=M=2 into the stated coefficient gives A=ε h, as required.

The three raw source digests match. Source 8effe5eb4947ba88 §4 (4)–(6) has the same actual continuation and localization. Source 26455afca6af9c16 §6 (13)–(16) gives the same tied derivative and continuous contact relation. Source d750a370b2e831ee §§1–4 supplies the signed envelope and finite-contact argument, and its §5 is the earlier regular fixed-normal application of the inverse equation.

Uses the same signed radial shell hypotheses to differentiate an optimized marked logarithmic objective. Its variational problem is different from the projective-energy envelope and the tied cap inverse.

initial_review.readability: The α_i expansion is a right derivative of the contact minimum. The inverse argument itself uses continuity and a positive proper-own coarea floor; it remains valid in the presence of other-fiber supporting incidences.
